title: Scores for Low-Performing Students Get Steadily Worse, and the Explanations Are Muddled
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler examines the 2019 NAEP science results, where falling scores among the lowest performers drove the decline, and shows that the officials interpreting them contradict one another. One blames too much time on reading and math, another blames too little time on reading. She argues the confusion comes from using one word, reading, for two different things, decoding and comprehension, and from assuming comprehension is a discrete skill rather than a product of background knowledge. Her prescription is a content-focused curriculum from kindergarten, separate testing of decoding and fluency, and better measures of socioeconomic status. The piece is a diagnosis of muddled thinking that ends in concrete recommendations for NAEP.
points: The head of NCES and a former NAEP board member offered seemingly contradictory explanations for the same decline, one saying too much reading and the other too little.
Decoding and comprehension are different processes, and testing does not identify students who need systematic phonics instruction.
More practice of comprehension skills with easy texts on random topics will likely keep scores low, because comprehension depends far more on academic knowledge than on general skills.
The NAEP Governing Board's own 2018 expert panel named the focus on comprehension skills as the cause of stagnant reading scores, yet officials keep ignoring it.
Free-lunch eligibility has become an unreliable income proxy, so reporting gaps only by race obscures the role of poverty and parental education.
quotes: Recent results from national science tests confirm a disturbing trend: scores are declining among the lowest-performing students. And those responsible for overseeing the tests are sending muddled messages about why that’s happening.
To figure that out, they would first need to understand that the term “reading” is being used to cover two very different processes: decoding, or sounding out, words; and understanding what you read.

Studies have shown that reading comprehension depends far more on academic knowledge than on generally applicable skills. So if schools want to boost reading comprehension, they should build students’ academic knowledge—and the vocabulary that goes with it—through a coherent, content-focused curriculum, beginning in kindergarten.

In fact, the NAEP Governing Board itself convened a panel of reading experts in 2018 that identified a focus on comprehension skills as the cause of stagnant reading scores. But NAEP officials apparently didn’t pay much attention, because Woodworth isn’t the only one who has made statements that seem to ignore or contradict it.

All this confusion stems from a fundamental lack of clarity not just about the definition of “reading” but also about what reading comprehension tests actually measure. The premise of reading tests like the NAEP is that comprehension can be measured as a discrete skill, despite evidence from cognitive science that it’s highly dependent on background knowledge.

Arguably, it never was all that reliable, since it lumped together different levels of poverty that could have significantly different implications for student outcomes. But more recently, a well-intentioned change in the regulations called the Community Eligibility Option has made it even less useful.
omitting any reference to income gives the impression that score gaps are all about race, when in fact they may well have more to do with poverty—or with parental level of education.
